 What Is a Mimic Panel? 2 Essential Types and Where They Work
 Long before every control room had a wall of screens, operators watched their plant on a single painted panel.
 The mimic panel still earns its place today as a simple, always on backup that a software screen cannot fully replace.
 Control Desk Display 
 Control Desk 
 Fire and Gas Safety 
 Printed vs Engraved 
 A mimic panel turns an entire plant layout into one picture an operator can read at a glance, no login required.
 Hello everyone, today we are going to learn about the mimic panel , what it is built from, the two common types, and where plants still rely on one.
 We will cover its construction, its role in fire and gas safety systems, how it compares with a software mimic screen, and where these panels are typically installed.
 Quick Answer
 What Is a Mimic Panel?
 A mimic panel is a pictorial representation of a plant process flow or system layout on the front of a control desk, with LED indicators lit at the exact spot where each piece of equipment sits.
 It works as an always visible backup that still shows plant status if the HMI screen fails, and is widely used for fire and gas safety systems.
 The two common types are printed panels , reverse printed on polycarbonate, and engraved panels , cut from plastic stock.
 What Is a Mimic Panel?
 A mimic panel pictorially represents a plant's process flow or system layout on the front of a control desk. It works as a fixed, always visible reference for the whole operating team.
 An operator glancing at the panel sees the same physical arrangement as the real plant. Lamps and indicators light up in the exact spot on the diagram where the equipment actually sits.
 Its real job is to act as a second level backup. If the primary HMI screen goes dark, the panel still shows plant status.
 That status keeps showing without needing power to a workstation, a network link, or any application still running in the background.
 This is also why many DCS control rooms keep one installed even after moving most operations to software.

 How a Mimic Panel Is Built
 The construction is simple by design, since the panel has to keep working for decades with almost no maintenance.
 1
 Front Surface
 Polycarbonate or polyester sheet with a protective acrylic overlay carries the printed or engraved diagram.
 2
 Indicator Lighting
 Super bright LEDs sit behind the diagram, readable from up to 100 meters away across a large control room.
 3
 Backplate
 Bakelite, composite panel, CRCA sheet or aluminum forms the rigid structure behind the front surface.
 4
 Mounting
 Screws secure the assembly into a matching cutout built into the control desk itself.
 2 Common Panel Types
 Printed Panels
 Reverse printed on 10 mil polycarbonate in customized colors and symbols, giving sharp detail at a lower unit cost.
 Engraved Panels
 Cut directly from plastic stock, with modern versions mounted using weatherproof adhesive instead of drilling into the desk.

 Mimic Panel Role in Fire and Gas Safety Systems
 Fire and gas panels lean heavily on this layout, since a delay reading the display during an emergency is not acceptable.
 A well designed panel follows the same alarm priority logic covered in our DCS alarm types guide .
 1
 Geographical layout. The panel shows the physical installation footprint, not just a logical diagram.
 2
 Hazard indicator lamps. Fire and gas detection points light up exactly where the sensor sits on the plant.
 3
 Equipment status. Fire water pumps and foam systems show running, standby or fault at a glance.
 4
 Shutdown push buttons. Operators can trigger a plant shutdown directly from the panel in an emergency.
 5
 Manual extinguish activation. Dedicated controls fire the manual extinguishing system when needed.
 6
 Guarded critical buttons. Physical guards over the most critical buttons prevent accidental operation.
 Why this matters. A guarded button and a lit lamp still work during a power dip that can freeze a software screen mid refresh.

 Physical Panel vs Software Mimic Screen
 Most new control rooms pair a physical panel with a software mimic screen rather than choosing only one.
 The two approaches complement each other more than they compete, and pairing them is standard practice on a modern SCADA system .

 Where These Panels Are Used

 Benefits and Limitations
 Benefits 
 Works without power to a computer, readable at a distance, immune to software crashes, and simple enough that new operators learn it in minutes.
 Limitations 
 Fixed once built, cannot show live trend data, and any plant modification means new artwork rather than a quick software edit.

 Mimic Panel Questions Engineers Ask
 What is the main purpose of a mimic panel?
 It gives operators an always on visual backup of plant status that works even if the main HMI screen fails.
 What is the difference between a printed and engraved panel type?
 Printed panels use reverse printed polycarbonate, while engraved panels are cut directly from plastic stock.
 Is this kind of panel still used with modern SCADA systems?
 Yes. Many control rooms keep one as a hardwired backup alongside their alarm management screens.
 How far can the panel be read from?
 The super bright LEDs behind the diagram are typically readable from up to 100 meters away.
 Which industries use these panels most often?
 Cement plants, railways, petrochemical plants, power stations, utilities and foundries all use them regularly.

 What We Learn Today
 A mimic panel pictorially represents a plant layout on a control desk as a hardwired backup to the main HMI.
 Printed and engraved are the two common construction types, each built from polycarbonate or plastic stock.
 Fire and gas systems lean on these panels for guarded shutdown buttons that keep working when software does not.
